\subsection{From database IDs to list-ordered positions}

List ordering makes the vectors assigned to one IVF centroid contiguous.
An input row has identifier $i\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$; coarse assignment
uses computed centroid scores with the mathematical target
\begin{equation}
 a(i)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0\leq\ell<n_{\rm list}}
       \|\Pi x_i-\mu_\ell\|_2^2.
 \label{eq:4-assignment}
\end{equation}
The implementation uses the numerical assignment path described above.
Primary and residual encoding do not subtract $\mu_{a(i)}$: list
membership restricts the search universe independently of those
reconstructions.

The builder sorts assignments together with input IDs. Let $\rho(p)$
be the input ID at sorted physical position $p$, and $o_\ell$ the start
of list $\ell$. The completed arrays satisfy
\begin{equation}
 0=o_0\leq o_1\leq\cdots\leq o_{n_{\rm list}}=N,
 \qquad p\in[o_\ell,o_{\ell+1})\Longrightarrow a(\rho(p))=\ell.
 \label{eq:4-offsets}
\end{equation}
Lower-bound searches find each list's first position; equal offsets
therefore mark an empty list:
\[
 o_\ell=o_{\ell+1}\Longleftrightarrow\text{list }\ell\text{ is empty}.
\]
Positions stay fixed in a completed index but can change after
rebuilding. All arrays use the same $\rho(p)$, and IDs map
$p\mapsto\rho(p)$ back to input rows. Two-pass add temporarily builds
$\rho^{-1}$ to write new encodings directly at their destination
(scatter). Primary ties use physical positions; final ties use database
IDs.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\input{variants/thesis2/figures/physical-layout}
\caption[Physical GPU index layout]{Physical GPU index layout (schematic).
IVF offsets delimit contiguous physical-position ranges. Independent ID,
word-group-major primary, row-major residual and correction arrays share
position $p$. Byte offsets are relative to each allocation; the illustration
implies neither interleaved allocation nor measured memory transactions.}
\label{fig:4-layout}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Exact addresses and representation widths}

The primary representation groups candidates by subspace. For primary
byte $Z[m,p]$, its address is
\[
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm byte}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\]
Final packing combines four subspace bytes of one vector into each word:
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf w[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{addr}_{\rm byte}(\mathsf w[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:4-primary-address}
\end{equation}
Here $j=0,\ldots,M/4-1$. $\text{word-layout build}\Longrightarrow M\bmod4=0$;
other $M$ are rejected, while a separate byte-layout compilation retains
the byte representation. Each array occupies $NM$ bytes; repacking
temporarily holds both copies, costing $2NM$. The one-pass builder
reorders existing codes (gather) into a vector-major $[N,M]$ array,
transposes it and repacks, freeing obsolete copies. Two-pass construction
scatters directly into subspace-major storage before the same repack.
The search-time lane mapping is discussed in \Cref{sec:5-3}.

Residual codes remain row-major, with $b_r=\lceil dB_r/8\rceil$ bytes per
vector. In the eight-bit configuration, coordinate $t$ of row $p$ is
at byte offset $pb_r+t$. In the four-bit path it is in byte
$pb_r+\lfloor t/2\rfloor$, with even coordinates in the low four bits
(low nibble) and odd coordinates in the high four bits (high nibble).
A four-byte correction per physical row stores
\begin{equation}
 \gamma[ p ]=2\langle\widehat p(x_{\rho(p)}),
                              \widehat r(x_{\rho(p)})\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-correction}
\end{equation}
The correction must move with its row's codes during gathering or
scattering. List-order scans can then fetch residuals only for retained
candidates. Refinement uses compressed reconstructions; raw FP32
reranking would require an additional $4Nd$ device bytes. Chapter 7
evaluates the resulting recall.

\subsection{Bounded input batches and two-pass construction}

Keeping whole-database raw and rotated arrays on the GPU would require
$4Nd+4Nd=8Nd$ bytes. Bounded staging limits these arrays while the
compressed index remains resident. For $n_b$ pipeline buffers,
configured add rows $a_{\rm add}$ and per-array budget $S_{\rm stage}$,
the staged row count and raw/rotated device storage are
\begin{equation}
 a_{\rm in}=\max\!\left\{1,\min\!\left(a_{\rm add},
 \left\lfloor\frac{S_{\rm stage}}{4d}\right\rfloor\right)\right\},
 \qquad S_{\rm float}=8n_ba_{\rm in}d.
 \label{eq:4-staging-rows}
\end{equation}
\[
 4d\leq S_{\rm stage},\quad n_b=3,\ S_{\rm stage}=128\,\mathrm{MiB}
 \Longrightarrow S_{\rm float}\leq2n_bS_{\rm stage}=768\,\mathrm{MiB}.
\]
The bound covers these floating-point arrays; assignment and encoder
scratch are additional. One-pass construction encodes rows in input
order and gathers them into list order. Two-pass construction first
assigns and orders rows, then rereads and encodes directly into their
final positions, trading an extra traversal for fewer compressed copies.

\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\centering
\input{variants/thesis2/figures/add-paths}
\captionof{figure}[One- and two-pass construction]{One- and two-pass construction.}
\label{fig:2-add-paths}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

For Stella, analytical row-array occupancy is 40.59\,GiB for one-pass gather and 21.32\,GiB for two-pass repack (\cref{tab:4-phase-storage}). One pass holds both input-order and list-order encodings; two passes write directly into list order. In the first assignment pass, centroids are transformed back with $\Pi^\top$, avoiding rotation of database rows.

\subsection{Memory use across construction phases}

The implementation estimates one-pass memory from the row arrays and
an allowance for other allocations:
\begin{equation}
 H_{\rm single}=N(2b_r+3M+20)+2^{30}\quad\text{bytes}.
 \label{eq:4-peak-heuristic}
\end{equation}
The ten live arrays contribute
\[
 3NM+2Nb_r+20N=N(3M+2b_r+20).
\]
The 1\,GiB allowance is heuristic. During final two-pass repacking,
IDs, residuals, corrections and two primary copies instead require
\begin{equation}
 S_{\rm repack,2}=N(b_r+2M+8).
 \label{eq:4-two-pass-repack}
\end{equation}
Whole-build peak also includes models, sorting, context, earlier
pipeline/inverse scratch and later query workspace. The phase values in
\Cref{tab:4-phase-storage} isolate row arrays, rather than whole-process
peaks.

Queries rotate, route, screen and refine to return $k$ IDs/scores. \Cref{fig:5-query-path} distinguishes the
three runtime selection decisions; the ground-truth ordering is an
external evaluation object.

Four quantities must be kept separate:
\begin{align}
 s_i(q)&=\|\mu_i\|_2^2-2\langle q',\mu_i\rangle,
                   &&\text{centroid routing score},\nonumber\\
 \primarydist(q,x)&=\|q'-\widehat p(x)\|_2^2,
                   &&\text{primary score},\nonumber\\
 \refineddist(q,x)&=\|q'-\widehat p(x)-\widehat r(x)\|_2^2
                       +\|q'\|_2^2,
                   &&\text{refined ranking score},\nonumber\\
 \rawdist(q,x)&=\|q-x\|_2^2,
                   &&\text{raw-space distance}.
 \label{eq:5-ranking-objects}
\end{align}
$\mu_i$ is a transformed centroid; $\widehat p,\widehat r$ are decoded primary/residual vectors. The runtime refined score includes a query-only
constant, as derived from the implemented correction in \Cref{sec:5-6}.
It preserves the ordering of reconstructed distances for a fixed query,
but neither it nor the primary score is the original-vector distance.

Subspace-major codes align neighbouring lanes/candidates; splitting reduces LUT storage.

\subsection{Address mapping and four-byte packing}

For list $\ell$, row $r$ maps to
\[
 p=o_\ell+r,\qquad \operatorname{offset}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\]
At fixed $m$, $\Delta\operatorname{offset}=\Delta p$. List boundaries can break adjacency.

Pack four subspace bytes per candidate:
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{w}[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm bytes}(\mathsf{w}[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:5-packed-layout}
\end{equation}
For $0\leq t<4$ and eight-bit $Z$,
\[
 (\mathsf w[j,p]\gg8t)\mathbin{\&}255=Z[4j+t,p].
\]
Nibbles index \cref{eq:5-lut-factorisation}.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\centering
\input{figures/ch5/packed-access}
\captionof{figure}[Packed candidate-parallel access]{Packed candidate-parallel access, showing a subset of warp lanes.
At fixed word group $j$, consecutive positions access adjacent four-byte
words. Each word contains four subspace codes of one candidate. Unpacking
preserves each code byte; LUT splitting happens afterwards. The diagram
illustrates addresses, not a measured number of memory transactions.}
\label{fig:5-packed-access}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

Construction maps $[M,N]$ bytes to $[M/4,N]$ words ($4\mid M$). Casting would combine candidate bytes. Code-byte costs:
\[
 R=W=NM,\qquad S_{\rm old+new}=2NM.
\]
Repacking is outside search timing.

\subsection{Memory traffic and score consistency}

One word load/unpack replaces four byte loads. The logical warp window is $32\times4=128$ bytes; transactions depend on alignment/active lanes. Payload stays $M$ bytes per candidate. Both tested layouts are subspace-major, so transpose/cache effects are not isolated.

Local top-$c$ can emit $\gscan c$ intermediate entries for $c$ winners. Shared bounds reduce this maintenance. The scheduler
then chooses how much scan parallelism to expose. Both operate at a fixed
refinement budget; choosing that budget is the separate problem in
\Cref{ch:refinement}.

\subsection{A complete-key upper bound with explicit witnesses}

Let $K_{(c)}$ be the global $c$th key when $|U|\geq c$. If a group holds
$c$ distinct, fully scored candidates, the largest key among those
witnesses, $\tau_j$, satisfies $K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_j$. There are already
$c$ candidates no later than $\tau_j$ in the global universe. The shared
bound is initialised to a top sentinel and updated by
\begin{equation}
 \tau\leftarrow\min_{\prec}(\tau,\tau_j).
 \label{eq:5-shared-update}
\end{equation}
No bound is published from fewer than $c$ valid candidates. If the entire
universe has fewer than $c$, no group can publish such a bound and all
valid candidates remain eligible.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Safe rejection by a witnessed bound]
\label{prop:5-shared-bound}
Assume fixed keys, publications backed by $c$ distinct candidates, and
reads that return either the initial sentinel or one complete published
key. Rejecting a candidate only when $K_q(x)\succ\tau$ cannot remove a
global top-$c$ candidate, irrespective of publication timing.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A publication has a set $W_\tau$ of $c$ distinct witnesses:
\[
 \max_{x\in W_\tau}K_q(x)\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{(c)}\preceq\tau.
\]
Sentinel reads and minima of published keys obey the same inequality. Thus
\[
 x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ K_q(x)\preceq K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_{\rm seen}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x\text{ is not rejected}.
\]
Stale reads only loosen the bound. Publications
made after earlier safe rejections remain valid: any $c$ retained
distinct candidates still supply $c$ witnesses, whether or not they are
the best $c$ of their group.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

Shared filtering retains global coverage (\cref{prop:5-local-coverage}). Admission is
\begin{equation}
 K_q(x)\prec\lambda_j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 K_q(x)\preceq\tau_{\rm seen},
 \label{eq:5-admission}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_j$ is the local compaction threshold and $\tau_{\rm seen}$ the last shared key read. The shared comparison retains equality.

\subsection{Publication, filtering and implementation limits}

For nonnegative FP32 scores, canonical positive zero and valid nonnegative positions,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa(D,p)=2^{32}\operatorname{uintbits}_{32}(D)+p.
 \label{eq:5-packed-key}
\end{equation}
On this non-NaN domain, monotone float bits give
\[
 (D_1,p_1)\prec(D_2,p_2)\iff\kappa(D_1,p_1)<\kappa(D_2,p_2).
\]
Finite keys precede infinity and the all-one sentinel. Invalid positions cannot publish.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\centering
\input{figures/ch5/shared-bound}
\captionof{figure}[Shared complete-key filtering]{Shared complete-key filtering for one scan group. A candidate's
full primary score is computed before admission. A valid $c$-candidate
witness set can tighten the per-query bound; a stale but complete bound
only weakens filtering. Final prefix trimming reduces the valid merge
input, while the allocated workspace capacity remains unchanged.
The whole-key-read premise is qualified in the text.}
\label{fig:5-shared-bound}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

A thread reads the shared bound once per scanned chunk. After compaction, $c$ valid keys permit 64-bit \texttt{atomicMin}. Final publication/search trims the prefix; exact merge handles stale extras. In-stream reset precedes scanning, then merging; groups never wait.

The whole-key premise uses aligned eight-byte strong PTX \path{ld.volatile.global.u64}/\path{atom.global.min.u64} \cite{ptx_isa}, beyond C++ \texttt{volatile} \cite{cuda_programming_guide}. CUDA 13.0.88 \texttt{ptxas}, \texttt{sm\_120} corroborates it; the driver's JIT-generated native GPU instructions (SASS) were not captured.

Filtering follows full primary scoring (\cref{fig:5-shared-bound}): maintenance savings compete with polling/atomics (\cref{sec:7-4}).

\subsection{Choosing parallelism without changing the budget}

$b\gscan$ blocks add parallelism and staging/selection/merge costs. Smaller quotas require a certificate or fallback. Concentrated pilot survivors motivated witnessed bounds (\cref{sec:7-4}).

Define
\[
 T_{\rm blk}=\text{scan threads/block},\quad
 H=n_{\rm SM}T_{\rm resident/SM},\quad
 v=\frac{\operatorname{sd}(n_c)}{\operatorname{mean}(n_c)}.
\] Its rule is
\begin{align}
 g_{\rm fill}
 &=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup
       \{h\in\{2,4,8\}:bhT_{\rm blk}\leq0.6H\}\right),
       \label{eq:5-fill-rule}\\
 g_{\rm skew}&=
   \begin{cases}4,&v\geq0.3,\\1,&v<0.3,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 g_{\rm chosen}=\max(g_{\rm fill},g_{\rm skew}).
 \label{eq:5-skew-rule}
\end{align}
The skew rule may override the fill limit. In the evaluation harness,
$v$ is calibrated using 512 database vectors as pseudoqueries and a
fixed routing configuration; it uses no ground-truth labels. This is
distinct from Chapter 6's sampled output-agreement calibration. Once
calibrated, scheduling uses the batch size and stored statistic without
an additional per-search host readback. The constants were fitted on
four pilot configurations and then evaluated on further configurations.
The one-time pseudoquery calibration is excluded from
the reported steady-state search times. Observed startup ranges, separate from refinement-budget calibration (\cref{sec:a-supplement}), are
\[
 T_{\rm gather}\in[0.81,7.04]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 T_{\rm first}\in[6.00,27.77]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 \operatorname{median}(T_{\rm repeat})\in[2.72,18.13]\,\mathrm{ms}.
\]

Choosing one group dispatches $\gscan=0$ at fixed index/probes/budget. Its distance-only ties need a common-order check for identical survivors. Integrated speedups and scheduling losses are in \cref{sec:7-6}.

\subsection{Observed execution paths}

On the 170-SM RTX 5090 (48 warps/SM) \cite{blackwell_tuning},
\[
 1000\cdot2\cdot512=1{,}024{,}000
 >0.6\cdot170\cdot48\cdot32=156{,}672.
\]
Fill therefore chooses one group; skew can override to four.

In E1, 9/38 records cross $v=0.3$, all Vogue ($0.338$--$0.622$). Its 27 cells use four groups; 105 arXiv/OpenAI cells use $\gscan=0$. Their gains use LUTs, packing, lanes and probe selection, without grouped retention/bounds.

Vogue: 3--15 pure-tie differences/1,000 queries, zero non-tie differences, identical final outputs. At 128 probes the tie range is 7--11.

Observed cell counts are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrr}
 &G=0&G=2&G=4\\\hline
 \text{held-out}&10&0&2\\
 S=128&2&8&2
 \end{array}
\]
Eight of twelve switch paths. Benefits depend on load size/skew, without a fixed batch-256 cutoff.

The heuristic omits residency/compaction/merge costs; pseudoqueries can age. Regret is the best tested fixed-group speedup divided by the scheduler's

\subsection{A complete-key upper bound with explicit witnesses}

Let $K_{(c)}$ be the global $c$th key when $|U|\geq c$. If a group holds
$c$ distinct, fully scored candidates, the largest key among those
witnesses, $\tau_j$, satisfies $K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_j$. There are already
$c$ candidates no later than $\tau_j$ in the global universe. The shared
bound is initialised to a top sentinel and updated by
\begin{equation}
 \tau\leftarrow\min_{\prec}(\tau,\tau_j).
 \label{eq:5-shared-update}
\end{equation}
No bound is published from fewer than $c$ valid candidates. If the entire
universe has fewer than $c$, no group can publish such a bound and all
valid candidates remain eligible.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Safe rejection by a witnessed bound]
\label{prop:5-shared-bound}
Assume fixed keys, publications backed by $c$ distinct candidates, and
reads that return either the initial sentinel or one complete published
key. Rejecting a candidate only when $K_q(x)\succ\tau$ cannot remove a
global top-$c$ candidate, irrespective of publication timing.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A publication has a set $W_\tau$ of $c$ distinct witnesses:
\[
 \max_{x\in W_\tau}K_q(x)\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{(c)}\preceq\tau.
\]
Sentinel reads and minima of published keys obey the same inequality. Thus
\[
 x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ K_q(x)\preceq K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_{\rm seen}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x\text{ is not rejected}.
\]
Stale reads only loosen the bound. Publications
made after earlier safe rejections remain valid: any $c$ retained
distinct candidates still supply $c$ witnesses, whether or not they are
the best $c$ of their group.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

Shared filtering retains global coverage (\cref{prop:5-local-coverage}). Admission is
\begin{equation}
 K_q(x)\prec\lambda_j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 K_q(x)\preceq\tau_{\rm seen},
 \label{eq:5-admission}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_j$ is the local compaction threshold and $\tau_{\rm seen}$ the last shared key read. The shared comparison retains equality.

\subsection{Publication, filtering and implementation limits}

For nonnegative FP32 scores, canonical positive zero and valid nonnegative positions,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa(D,p)=2^{32}\operatorname{uintbits}_{32}(D)+p.
 \label{eq:5-packed-key}
\end{equation}
On this non-NaN domain, monotone float bits give
\[
 (D_1,p_1)\prec(D_2,p_2)\iff\kappa(D_1,p_1)<\kappa(D_2,p_2).
\]
Finite keys precede infinity and the all-one sentinel. Invalid positions cannot publish.

\subsection{Choosing parallelism without changing the budget}

$b\gscan$ blocks add parallelism and staging/selection/merge costs. Smaller quotas require a certificate or fallback. Concentrated pilot survivors motivated witnessed bounds (\cref{sec:7-4}).

Define
\[
 T_{\rm blk}=\text{scan threads/block},\quad
 H=n_{\rm SM}T_{\rm resident/SM},\quad
 v=\frac{\operatorname{sd}(n_c)}{\operatorname{mean}(n_c)}.
\] Its rule is
\begin{align}
 g_{\rm fill}
 &=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup
       \{h\in\{2,4,8\}:bhT_{\rm blk}\leq0.6H\}\right),
       \label{eq:5-fill-rule}\\
 g_{\rm skew}&=
   \begin{cases}4,&v\geq0.3,\\1,&v<0.3,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 g_{\rm chosen}=\max(g_{\rm fill},g_{\rm skew}).
 \label{eq:5-skew-rule}
\end{align}
The skew rule may override the fill limit. In the evaluation harness,
$v$ is calibrated using 512 database vectors as pseudoqueries and a
fixed routing configuration; it uses no ground-truth labels. This is
distinct from Chapter 6's sampled output-agreement calibration. Once
calibrated, scheduling uses the batch size and stored statistic without
an additional per-search host readback. The constants were fitted on
four pilot configurations and then evaluated on further configurations.
The one-time pseudoquery calibration is excluded from
the reported steady-state search times. Observed startup ranges, separate from refinement-budget calibration (\cref{sec:a-supplement}), are
\[
 T_{\rm gather}\in[0.81,7.04]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 T_{\rm first}\in[6.00,27.77]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 \operatorname{median}(T_{\rm repeat})\in[2.72,18.13]\,\mathrm{ms}.
\]

Choosing one group dispatches $\gscan=0$ at fixed index/probes/budget. Its distance-only ties need a common-order check for identical survivors. Integrated speedups and scheduling losses are in \cref{sec:7-6}.

\subsection{Observed execution paths}

On the 170-SM RTX 5090 (48 warps/SM) \cite{blackwell_tuning},
\[
 1000\cdot2\cdot512=1{,}024{,}000
 >0.6\cdot170\cdot48\cdot32=156{,}672.
\]
Fill therefore chooses one group; skew can override to four.

In E1, 9/38 records cross $v=0.3$, all Vogue ($0.338$--$0.622$). Its 27 cells use four groups; 105 arXiv/OpenAI cells use $\gscan=0$. Their gains use LUTs, packing, lanes and probe selection, without grouped retention/bounds.

Vogue: 3--15 pure-tie differences/1,000 queries, zero non-tie differences, identical final outputs. At 128 probes the tie range is 7--11.

Observed cell counts are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrr}
 &G=0&G=2&G=4\\\hline
 \text{held-out}&10&0&2\\
 S=128&2&8&2
 \end{array}
\]
Eight of twelve switch paths. Benefits depend on load size/skew, without a fixed batch-256 cutoff.

The heuristic omits residency/compaction/merge costs; pseudoqueries can age. Regret is the best tested fixed-group speedup divided by the scheduler's
speedup; its worst measured value is 1.217 at batch 256. Budgets stay fixed; \cref{sec:5-6} handles refinement.

\subsection{重建评分与查询常数}

对 $\gamma=2\langle\widehat p,\widehat r\rangle$，按实数算术展开：
\begin{align}
 \refineddist(q,x)
 &=\primarydist(q,x)+\|q'-\widehat r(x)\|_2^2+\gamma(x)
 \label{eq:5-refined-score}\\
 &=2\|q'\|_2^2+\|\widehat p+\widehat r\|_2^2-2\langle q',\widehat p+\widehat r\rangle\nonumber\\
 &=\|q'-\widehat p(x)-\widehat r(x)\|_2^2+\|q'\|_2^2.
 \label{eq:5-refined-constant}
\end{align}
该查询常数保持重建距离顺序 \cite{jhq}。

\subsection{最终选择与数值边界}

在至少有 $k$ 个有限、有效且 ID 唯一的保留候选时，每轮计算
\[
 i^*=\arg\min_{i<c}(D_{H,i},\mathrm{ID}_i),\quad d^*=D_{H,i^*},\quad
 D_{H,i^*}\leftarrow+\infty
\]
使用全部槽位，输出 $(\mathrm{ID}_{i^*},d^*)$：这是保留池内精确的 top-$k$，没有线程配额。不足额池可能在无穷距离处重复最小有效 ID；全无效池返回无效 ID。测试配置满足有限项前提。

主码并列使用位置，最终并列使用 ID。路由排除／量化仍存在；lane FP32 结合顺序可能改变近并列结果。
